Beneath it sit the carotenoids, the same family of compounds that colors carrots and egg yolks. Trapped sugar, bright light, and cool nights are the recipe. A warm, cloudy, wet autumn produces little red; a run of sunny days and near-freezing nights produces a great deal.

One theory holds that the anthocyanins act as a sunscreen, shielding the leafs machinery while it dismantles itself and pulls nitrogen back into the branch for next year. Another holds that the red is a warning to insects looking for a place to lay its eggs.

[5] So the yellow is subtraction and the red is addition. A dull year is not a sick forest, it is usually a mild, wet October in which the tree had no reason to make anything new. A brilliant one is a forest that has been briefly starved of warmth and flooded with light, and has responded the only way it can.

On the hill farms where she works, some walls of this kind has stood for two centuries, and she can usually tell, from the way the stones are set, which of them will stand for two more.

[2] A dry-stone wall is not a pile. It is two walls leaning against each other, built in courses from a wide footing to a narrow top, with the gap between them packed tight with small rubble called hearting. [A] Every few feet a long stone the through is laid across the whole width to tie the two faces together. [B] Without throughs, the faces drift apart under their own weight, and the wall totally bites it. [C] Delgado says she can spot a wall built without them from the road, the way a doctor spots a limp. [D]

[3] The work looks slow because it is. Delgado handles each stone once if she can and twice if she must; she picks it up, turns it, and setting it, and if it does not sit, she does not force it. "The stone tells you where it goes," she says. "Your job is to listen faster." A good waller builds about three meters a day. A hurried one builds five and comes back in ten years to do it again.

[4] Most of her work now is repair. Farmers call when a section has slumped after a wet spring or a tractor has clipped a corner, and she rebuilds it from the footing up, reusing every stone she can. She rarely brings new stone to a job, the old stone is already the right color, already weathered, and already shaped by whomever built the wall the first time. Her repairs are meant to disappear.

[5] Asked whether she minds that nobody will know which sections are her's, she laughs. "A wall that gets noticed is a wall that's failing," she says. My mother, who had grown up beside a lake and could not remember not knowing how, finally signed me up for adult lessons at the municipal pool, where nobody I knew would see me holding a kickboard.

[2] The instructor was a retired lifeguard named Mr. Osei, and his first lesson had nothing to do with strokes. He asked each of us to put our faces in the water and blow bubbles until they ran out of breath. [A] Most of the class managed it on the first try. I lasted about two seconds before I stood up, gasping, certain I had nearly bit the dust in three feet of water. [B] Mr. Osei did not laugh. He told me that the body's panic at having it's face covered is older than any of us, and that the only cure for it was repetition. [C] Every evening that week I filled the bathroom sink, set a timer, and put my face in until the beeping told me I could stop. [D]

[3] By the second lesson I could float on my back, an achievement that felt more like surrender than skill. Floating, it turned out, asked nothing of me except that I stop fighting the water. The strokes came slowly after that. My arms, which had spent fourteen years pulling doors and carrying groceries, was not used to pulling something that gave way. I swallowed a great deal of the pool.

[4] The test at the end of the course was a single length of the deep end. I remember the moment the floor dropped away beneath me and the water turned from pale green to a blue that seemed to go down forever and never end. My hand hit the far wall at last. Breathing hard, Mr. Osei wrote something on his clipboard while I hung there, and then he nodded once.

[5] I still am not a graceful swimmer. Even so, I know the difference between fear and danger now, and that the two are not always in the same place. The pool taught me that, it was never trying to hurt me, it was only waiting for me to stop thrashing.

options.A: No, because the essay is chiefly about the embarrassment of learning to swim late, and the lessons themselves are barely described.
options.B: Yes, because it is organized lesson by lesson, describing the stroke that Mr. Osei introduced in each session of the course.
options.C: Yes, because it centers on Mr. Osei's advice about repetition, shows the narrator acting on it every evening, and presents the final swim as the result.

[1] In much of the world, the most important shopping happens after dark. The night market, a street or square that fills with food stalls and vendors from dusk until well past midnight, exist in some form from Bangkok to Marrakesh to Mexico City. It is easy to mistake it for a tourist attraction, and in a few cities it has become one. But the night market is older than tourism, it answers a need that the daytime shop never did.

[2] The first need is simply heat. In hot climates, the middle of the day is for shade and sleep, and commerce waits for the air to get better. Opening at six in the evening, novelty is not the point of such a market; it is a sensible adaptation, the same one that puts the siesta in the afternoon. The second need is time. For most of history, most people worked from first light until the light gave out, and the only hours that belonged to them came after. A market that met them in those hours met them in the only ones they had.

[3] What the night market sells, in the end, is not mainly goods. A shopper who wanted a shirt could buy one more cheaply and more quietly during the day. What the market offers is the crowd itself: the noise, the smoke from the grills, the chance to eat standing up beside a stranger, the sense of a whole neighborhood out of doors at once. In many places it is where families go on a weeknight, where teenagers are first allowed out alone, and a person who lives alone can eat dinner surrounded by people.

[4] Nevertheless, efforts to tidy the night market so often kill it. When a city moves the stalls indoors, gives each vendor a numbered booth, and closes their doors at ten, it keeps the food and loses the market. What was an event becomes a food court. The vendors are the same; the customers are the same; only the reason to go is gone.

[5] The night market persists where it is left alone, or nearly so. It survives the supermarket, the shopping mall, and the delivery app, because none of them offers what it does. They sell things. It sells the evening.

[1] Every autumn, having driven for hours to look at leaves, the question of what they are looking at stumps most people. The reds and yellows of October are not, as many assume, a kind of decay. They are the result of two different processes, one of them a revealing and the other a manufacturing, and the difference explains why some years are brilliant and others are dull.

[2] The yellow was there all summer. A leaf contains several pigments, and chlorophyll, the green one, are simply the most abundant. Beneath it sit the carotenoids, the same family of compounds that colors carrots and egg yolks. [A] In summer the tree constantly and continually replaces its chlorophyll, which breaks down quickly in sunlight. [B] As days shorten, the tree stops making the replacement, the green fades over a week or two, and the yellow that was always underneath comes into view. [C] Nothing new has been made. A curtain has been drawn back. [D]

[3] The red is different. Red comes from anthocyanins, pigments that most leaves do not contain in summer at all. Similarly, the tree makes them fresh in autumn, using sugars that the leaf produced during the day but could not send back into the branch, because a layer of cork cells has begun to seal the leaf off at its stem. Trapped sugar, bright light, and cool nights are the recipe. A warm, cloudy, wet autumn produces little red; a run of sunny days and near-freezing nights produces a great deal.

[4] Why a tree would spend energy coloring leaves it is about to drop remains an open question. One theory holds that the anthocyanins act as a sunscreen, shielding the leafs machinery while it dismantles itself and pulls nitrogen back into the branch for next year. Another holds that the red is a warning to insects looking for a place to lay its eggs.

[5] So the yellow is subtraction and the red is addition. A dull year is not a sick forest, it is usually a mild, wet October in which the tree had no reason to make anything new. A brilliant one is a forest that has been briefly starved of warmth and flooded with light, and has responded the only way it can.

I swallowed a great deal of the pool.

[4] The test at the end of the course was a single length of the deep end. I remember the moment the floor dropped away beneath me and the water turned from pale green to a blue that seemed to go down forever and never end. My hand hit the far wall at last. Breathing hard, Mr. Osei wrote something on his clipboard while I hung there, and then he nodded once.

[5] I still am not a graceful swimmer. Even so, I know the difference between fear and danger now, and that the two are not always in the same place. The pool taught me that, it was never trying to hurt me, it was only waiting for me to stop thrashing.
